lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Antisthenes and Crates, we're at leisure. So why don't we head straight for the descent, take a stroll, and watch the new arrivals — what they're like and what each one's doing?

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: Let's go, Diogenes. It'd be a pleasant sight to see some of them crying, others begging to be released, and a few barely coming down even as Hermes shoves them by the neck, still resisting and bracing themselves backwards — all for nothing.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: I'll tell you what I saw on the way down.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: Tell us, Crates. Sounds like you saw something hilarious.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Plenty of others were coming down with us, but the notable ones were Ismenodorus, the rich man from our city, Arsaces the satrap of Media, and Oroetes the Armenian. Ismenodorus — killed by robbers near Cithaeron on his way to Eleusis, I think — was groaning, clutching his wound, calling out to the infants he'd left behind, and blaming himself for his boldness. He crossed Cithaeron and those war-torn, deserted areas around Eleutherae with only two servants, while carrying five gold cups and four bowls.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Arsaces — already old, and by Zeus not bad-looking — was furious in that barbarian way, indignant at walking on foot, and demanded his horse be brought to him. His horse had died with him, both run through by a single thrust from a Thracian peltast in the skirmish on the Araxes against the Cappadocian. He was charging far ahead of the others, as he told it. The Thracian ducked under the shield, shook off Arsaces' spear, then planted his sarissa and skewered both him and the horse.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: How's that possible with one blow, Crates?

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Easy, Antisthenes. He's charging with this twenty-cubit spear out in front. The Thracian parries with the shield, the point goes past him, he drops to one knee, takes the charge on the sarissa, and the horse impales itself under the chest from its own speed and fury. And Arsaces gets run through from the groin straight through to the backside. You see? It was the horse's doing more than the man's. Still, he was indignant — equal rank to the others — and insisted on riding down.

lines.speaker: Crates
lines.text: Oroetes had the softest feet you ever saw, couldn't even stand on the ground, let alone walk. All Medes are like that when they get off their horses — they tiptoe as if stepping on thorns. So when he threw himself down and wouldn't get up for anything, good old Hermes just picked him up and carried him to the ferry. I laughed.

lines.speaker: Antisthenes
lines.text: When I came down, I didn't mix with the others. I left them wailing and ran ahead to the ferry, grabbed a good seat for a comfortable sail. The whole crossing they were crying and getting seasick, but I was enjoying it immensely.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You two had some colorful fellow travelers. Mine were Blepsias the moneylender from Pisa, Lampis the Acarnanian guide, and Damis the rich Corinthian. Damis poisoned by his own son. Lampis slit his throat over Myrtium the courtesan. Blepsias the poor wretch starved to death — looked it too, pale as a ghost and thin as a rail. I knew, but I asked them anyway how they died. To Damis blaming his son: "You got what was coming, if you've got a thousand talents, living it up at ninety, and you're handing an eighteen-year-old four obols." And you, Acarnanian — he was groaning and cursing Myrtium — "Why blame Love? Blame yourself. Never flinched from enemies, fought in the front lines like a maniac, but taken down by some little tart with fake tears and sighs, you big hero." Blepsias was already blaming himself for the stupidity of hoarding money for heirs who meant nothing to him, thinking he'd live forever, the fool. Anyway, their groaning gave me no small pleasure.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: But we're at the entrance now. We should look out and watch the arrivals from a distance. Good grief, so many, all sorts, and all crying — except these newborns and infants. Even the really old men are wailing. What's this? Is the love of life still got them?

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: I want to ask this very old man. Why are you crying at your age, having died? What's the indignation, my good fellow, and you an old man? Surely you were a king or something?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Not at all.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: A satrap then?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Not that either.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: So you were rich, and now it's upsetting you to die and leave all that luxury behind?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Nothing of the sort. I was about ninety, lived a hand-to-mouth life fishing with rod and line, dirt poor, no children, lame, and half-blind.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: And being like that, you still wanted to live?

lines.speaker: Old Pauper
lines.text: Yes. The light was sweet, and dying is terrible, something to be avoided.

lines.speaker: Diogenes
lines.text: You're out of your mind, old man, playing the youth with death, and at the ferryman's age. What can you even say about the young ones, when men your age are so in love with life — men who ought to be chasing death as a cure for the miseries of old age. But let's move on now, before someone suspects us of planning an escape, hanging around the mouth like this.
